body:
([recording](https://youtu.be/jpm9ojBUaP4))

We mostly discussed freshness evaluation. Here is the meeting summary.

1.  For tracking the refresh state for the source MV [2], the consensus is option 2 (treating source MV as a materialized table) which would give engines the flexibility on freshness determination (recursive beyond source MV or not).
2.  Earlier design doc [3] discussed max staleness config. But it wasn't reflected in the spec PR. The general opinion is to add the config to the spec PR. The open question is whether the \`materialization.max-staleness-ms\` config should be added to the view metadata or the storage table metadata. Either can work. We just need to decide which makes a little better fit.
3.  Prashanth brought up schema change with default value and how it may affect the MV refresh state (for SQL representation with select *). Jan mentioned that snapshot contains schema id when the snapshot was created. Engine can compare the snapshot schema id to the source table schema id during freshness evaluation. There is no need for additional schema info in refresh-state tracking in the storage table.
4.  Prashanth brought up another scenario of compaction/rewrite where a new snapshot was added with actual data change. The general take is that the engine can optimize and decide that MV is fresh as the new snapshot doesn't have any data change.

We can add some clarifications in the spec PR for freshness evaluation based on the above discussions.

[2] <https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_StBW5hCQhumhIvgbdsHjyW0ED3dWMkjtNzyPp9Sfr8/edit?tab=t.0>

[3] [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1UnhldHhe3Grz8JBngwXPA6ZZord1xMedY5ukEhZYF-A/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.3wigecex0zls](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1UnhldHhe3Grz8JBngwXPA6ZZord1xMedY5ukEhZYF-A/edit#heading=h.3wigecex0zls)

body:
([recording](https://youtu.be/Kn00iW1Rb8U))

We mostly discussed the \`max-staleness-ms\` config

**Q. Should we add the \`max-staleness-ms\` config?**

> **stale** -- The \`snapshot_id\`s do not match for at-least one source table, indicating that a refresh operation needs to be performed to capture the latest source table changes.

Currently, the spec PR only supports strict interpretation of staleness. Many MV use cases (like ETL) can allow some delay in MV refresh. Adding this config would enable those use cases.

The consensus is to add this config.

**Q. Should the config be defined in view or storage metadata?**

This config is part of the view definition. Also when the view is just created with the config via DDL, the storage table doesn’t exist yet. View metadata is the only right place to store this config.

The consensus is to add this config to the view metadata.

**Q. How should the \`max-staleness-ms\`  be interpreted?**

How should the staleness time be calculated ?

1.  Start from the time when the last refresh operation was started.
2.  Start from the earliest snapshot timestamp from any source table with snapshots added after the last MV refresh.

E.g., let’s assume the config is 60 mins.

  - 10:00 is when the last refresh operation was started.
  - 10:45 is the time when a source table has a new snapshot added.
  - At 11:15, is the MV still fresh? With option 1, it is stale. With option 2, it is fresh.

Need more community input. We should also check how other databases/systems interpret this config.

**Q. If we choose the staleness time calculation based on source table’s new snapshot timestamp, do we still need the** **refresh-start-timestamp-ms** **in the refresh-state of the storage table?**

Yes, it is good information regardless of the decision on staleness time calculation.
title: Materialized View Sync notes, 2025-10-29

body:
([recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZdUoeGOltkM))

**Recap of the previous meeting on Oct 29**

  - Add the \`max-staleness-ms\` config that can benefit many MV use cases where some staleness is acceptable.
  - The config should be defined in the view object (not the storage table). It can be a metadata field (like \`storage-table\`) in the view definition.

**Q. \`target staleness\` vs \`max staleness\`?**

There are different wording for the staleness config. BigQuery uses \`target staleness\`. Snowflake uses \`target staleness\`. Trino uses \`grace period\`.

\`max staleness\` declares the intention of the MV creator, while \`target staleness\` is more related to engine refresh behavior. The consensus is staying with \`max staleness\`.

We can discuss the best choice of wording in the spec PR that is intuitive and reflects the purpose of “max staleness”.

**Q. How should the \`max-staleness\` config be interpreted?**

Igor proposed the **delayed view semantics**: “A Materialized View(MV) considered fresh if and only if the precomputed result from the storage table is equivalent to what would have been obtained by running MV's defining query at **some** point in time within the interval of [CurrentTime - MaxStaleness, CurrentTime]”.

E.g., let’s assume the config is 60 mins.

  - 10:00 is when the last refresh operation was started.
  - 10:45 is the time when a source table has a new snapshot added.
  - At 11:15, is the MV still fresh?

In the example from the previous meeting, the delayed view semantics would render the MV fresh at 11:15. Within the interval of [10:15, 11:15], there exists **some** point in time (like 10:30) where the precomputed result from the storage table would be the same to run the MV definition SQL directly.

There is broad support for the delayed view semantic above and the principle that spec should be permissive to enable engines more flexibility for implementations and optimizations. E.g.

  - If the 10:45 commit in a source table is a \`replace\` operation for compaction, engines can be smart and decide that the MV is still fresh at 11:15.
  - Another unusual scenario. At 10:30, a data file was added to the source table. At 10:45, the same data file was removed from the source table. There is no net change after the two commits. Engines can decide that the MV is still fresh at 11:15.

This definition is also aligned with many engine implementations today, like [Snowflake](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/dynamic-tables-target-lag), [Trino](https://trino.io/docs/current/connector/iceberg.html#materialized-views).

**Q. How should clients or engines behave if the MV is stale?**

The spec can suggest the following behaviors if MV is stale

  - May fail the query.
  - May perform inline refresh **without** updating the storage table.
  - May perform inline refresh **and** update the storage table.

Simple clients (like Python library) may not understand the view SQL and can choose to fail if MV is stale.

Some engines can perform inline refresh to avoid failing the queries. If engines also update the storage table, it is up to engine implementation to handle concurrent refresh. E.g., maybe use locks to coordinate and avoid concurrent wasteful concurrent refreshes and updates. Iceberg MV spec won’t define the refresh and storage table update behavior.

**Q. Should Iceberg MV support non-Iceberg source tables or views (like Hive, Postgres)?**

The consensus is to limit the initial scope of MV to Iceberg source tables and views so that we can get the initial version of the Iceberg MV spec out.

There are additional complexities with non-Iceberg sources like Hive, Postgres, etc.

  - Current storage tables refresh-state uses \`uuid\` to identify the source table or view. \`uuid\` is only an Iceberg concept.
  - How to evaluate the state for non-Iceberg source tables? They can always be assumed as there are data changes, since we don’t know how to evaluate the source table state. This will fall back to evaluating the staleness based on the last refresh. Hence, this still works with the delayed view semantic.

We can revisit the topic and potentially expand the scope in the future.

body:
([recording](https://youtu.be/ZshN590NOxk))

Recapped the key points raised by Walaa and Benny against the previous proposal on handling nested MVs - only store source MV’s storage table and let consumers decide recursive evaluation or not.

  - smart producers and dumb consumers
  - producer ... use two flat lists of source views and source tables
  - Freshness evaluation becomes inconsistent
  - recursion for freshness does not align with recursion for refresh

A revised proposal is discussed and has the consensus in the meeting

  - Producers generate two flat lists of source table states and source view states.

      - Producers are allowed to express the consumption policy by storing a subset of the base views, tables, MVs.
      - Producers may expand nested MVs recursively in the refresh state.
      - Producers can generate empty lists too. (non Iceberg sources like Postgres, Delta, Hive)
  - Consumers are required to at least perform coarse-grained freshness evaluation based on the refresh-start-timestamp-ms field from refresh state and the max-staleness config.
  - Consumers may additionally compare the two flat lists (source-view-state and source-table-state) populated by the producer against the states loaded from catalog. A MV can still be considered fresh after this evaluation even if the refresh-start-timestamp-ms  is out of the max-staleness window.
  - For the use case that MVs are always considered fresh, the max-staleness config can be set to Long.MAX_VALUE.
  - The refresh state (view or table) must include the names in addition to the UUID, as consumers can only load view or table objects from catalog by names. Dumb consumers (like Python clients) may not be able to parse SQL and figure out the referenced view or table names.

Benny’s notes

- producer stores a refresh state that is non-recursive when it comes to nested MVs.  So, the refresh state is two lists of views and tables where tables can be either a source table or storage table.  We will also include view and table paths (namespace + name) for simple consumers who can't parse SQLs or lookup identifiers by uuid.  Including refresh state is optional for producers but refresh-start-timestamp-ms is required.

- consumers have 3 high level ways of freshness validation:

1.  decide based on refresh-start-timestamp-ms alone.. such as being within max-staleness-ms.  The cool thing about this is that it enables non-Iceberg tables in views.

2.  iterate through refresh state lists but no SQL parsing.  For source tables, validate timestamps on the last data changing snapshot.  For storage tables, consumers can decide whether to further expand the storage table refresh state or just validate the storage table's last update time.  For views, validate versions didn't change.

3.  consumer parses MV SQL to validate query tree is valid.. besides this, is there any additional benefit to parsing SQL that we don't get with 2?  Maybe I'm missing something here.
title: Materialized View Sync notes, 2025-12-10

body:
([recording](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZwjOMrf1eg))

A revised proposal is discussed and has the consensus in the meeting

  - Producers update the refresh state in storage table.

      - Producers are allowed to express the consumption policy by storing a subset of the base views, tables, MVs.
      - Producers may expand nested MVs recursively in the refresh state.
      - Producers can generate empty lists too. This can help with non Iceberg sources like Postgres, Delta, Hive.
      - If can’t capture source state for all source tables, the source table list should be empty
      - Leaning toward a single list with a type field. If a single list, should MV be one or two entries in this single list? Two entries for now
  - Consumers are required to at least perform coarse-grained freshness evaluation based on the refresh-start-timestamp-ms field from refresh state and the max-staleness config.
  - Consumers may additionally compare the two flat lists (source-view-state and source-table-state) populated by the producer against the states loaded from catalog. A MV can still be considered fresh after this evaluation even if the refresh-start-timestamp-ms  is out of the max-staleness window.
  - For the use case that MVs are always considered fresh, the max-staleness config can be set to Long.MAX_VALUE.
  - The refresh state (view or table) must include the names in addition to the UUID, as consumers can only load view or table objects from catalog by names. Dumb consumers (like Python clients) may not be able to parse SQL and figure out the referenced view or table names.
  - For term definitions (like fresh), validate with other platforms for consistency
  - Should define consumer behavior if a MV is evaluated to be stale?

      - Can fail, or refresh inline, or treat MV as a logical view
      - Mustn’t consume from the storage table
  - What should consumers do if a MV is invalid?

      - Adopt the same language as view, leave out the invalid state term. View spec doesn’t define invalid state (like schema changed)
title: Materialized View Sync notes, 2025-12-16

body:
([recording](https://youtu.be/U6DhyxKRIXw))

Questions from Benny

1.  Should we separate the nested MVs into its own list in the refresh state?  (It's a tuple of view + storage table)  A producer may find a nested MV but choose not to use the materialization and instead directly query the view for the latest data.  I think this is a cleaner data model for the consumer than to mix up expanded views and views with materializations that the producer used.

2.  I'm not sure if having max-staleness-ms property is a good idea to include in the spec when its interpretation is so open.  If we really wanted to have such a property and prescribe how it should be used, we'd need multiple variations like:  max-staleness-for-refresh-start-comparison, max-staleness-for-source-table-comparison, max-staleness-for-storage-table-comparison, etc.

3. Should the producer include a max-staleness config for each source table state?

Questions from Steven

  - Can consumers load MV storage tables directly from catalog for freshness evaluation?
  -  How to expose MV via REST catalog?

      - Can take 3 round-trips: load table (), load view, load storage table
      - loadTableOrView API for one round trip
      - A single load call might also be easier for access control.
      - What about non-REST catalogs?
  - How to encode the source table states the [diamond shape pattern](https://docs.google.com/document/d/1_StBW5hCQhumhIvgbdsHjyW0ED3dWMkjtNzyPp9Sfr8/edit?tab=t.0) if the producer decides to recursively refresh nested MVs? Need lineage path information in the nested MV source tables?

Key takeaways

  - There will be a single combine list in the refresh state of MV storage tables. To start with, there will be two types of entries in the list: view and table.

      - A nested MV could have two entries in the list: one for view state and one for storage table state.
      - If a producer wants non-recursive interpretation, it may exclude the nested MV’s storage table in the list and include recursive source tables in the list.
  - Consumers should be able to load MV storage tables directly from the catalog.

      - In the future, if the catalog supports combined loading to reduce the round trips to load a MV and its storage table, we may revisit the list type and include a third type for materialized-view.
  - For nested MVs (including diamond shape problem) evaluation, <[email removed]> will write down the scenarios, expected consumer and producer behaviors.
  - If the snapshot id from the refresh state is not found in table state loaded from catalog (e.g. purged due to snapshot retention), consumers can fail the query, treat the view as logical view, etc.
  - We are close to a point where a reference implementation may be needed to validate the design choices before the MV spec can be finally approved.
